viva.summary: The student understands the high-level purpose of the linked list operations but lacks a deep understanding of pointer manipulation and edge-case handling. They struggled to explain the mechanics of the dummy node and the slow/fast pointer logic.

rubric.revise_next: Review how dummy nodes simplify linked list deletions and practice tracing pointer movements on paper with small lists.

questions.answer: The dummy node is just there to store the size of the list as an integer. It is necessary because the code will crash if you do not have a zero at the front to initialize the counter.
questions.feedback: The dummy node is used to handle edge cases like removing the head node, not for storing the list size.
questions.prompt: In your `remove_all` function, what is the purpose of `dummy = Node(0)` and why is it necessary for the logic to work correctly?

questions.answer: The result is 20 because the fast pointer goes to the end and the slow one stays in the middle. I am not really sure how many steps they take though.
questions.feedback: You correctly identified the output, but you need to trace the pointer movement more precisely to understand the algorithm.
questions.prompt: What would be the output of calling middle(from_list([10, 20]))? Explain how your slow and fast pointers move to reach that result.

questions.answer: I think I should change the loop condition to stop when fast.next is None or fast.next.next is None instead.
questions.feedback: Your suggestion is a bit vague; consider how changing the loop condition affects when the slow pointer stops relative to the fast pointer.
questions.prompt: If you wanted to modify the middle function to return the first middle node instead of the second one for even-length lists, what single logical change would you make to the loop condition or pointer movement?
